To produce and maintain a directed motion, there must also be a force acting on the charged particles in a particular direction.
A force is a push or pull that can change motion.
Directed motion here means a continuing net movement along a direction, not that every particle follows a smooth, straight path.
resolvedSectionBreaks.after:
An electric field describes the electric push or pull on charge at each place.
The force exerted by this field on a charged particle satisfies $\vec{F}=q\vec{E}.$

resolvedSectionBreaks.before:
Electrostatic equilibrium means that mobile charge has settled into an arrangement with no continuing directed flow.
Inside an ordinary conductor in this state, the electric field is zero.
This equilibrium statement cannot be applied to an ordinary conductor that is carrying a steady conduction current.
resolvedSectionBreaks.after:
Potential difference is also called voltage.
It compares the energy transferred per amount of charge between two places.
Electric potential compares a place with a chosen reference, and the difference between two potentials gives their voltage.

resolvedSectionBreaks.before:
Mobile electrons in a metal drift in the opposite direction.
The following demonstration compares potentials along a conductor.
resolvedSectionBreaks.after:
The historical demonstration uses a damp wooden strip suspended horizontally as a conductor.
Damp wood conducts less readily than a good metal conductor, but it can still conduct charge.
The apparatus described here is not a home wiring or high-voltage handling instruction.
